statement: Four litres of a solution that is 25 percent acid are mixed with six litres of a solution that is 50 percent acid. What percentage of the mixture is acid?

choices.misconception: I averaged 25 and 50 without weighting by how much of each solution there was.
I added the two percentages together, which cannot be right because a mixture can never be stronger than its strongest ingredient.
I weighted the percentages by the wrong volumes, giving the 25 percent solution the larger share.
I used only the acid from the weaker solution and spread it over all ten litres.

hints: Percentages only average when the amounts match.
Work out how many litres of pure acid are in each solution, then add them.
0.25 x 4 = 1 litre and 0.50 x 6 = 3 litres, so 4 litres of acid in 10 litres of mixture, which is 40 percent.

solutions.reliable: Track the acid itself rather than the percentages. The first solution contributes 0.25 x 4 = 1 litre of acid; the second contributes 0.50 x 6 = 3 litres. Together that is 4 litres of acid in 4 + 6 = 10 litres of mixture, so the concentration is 4/10 = 40 percent. The transferable idea: a weighted average always lands nearer the ingredient you used more of - here nearer 50 than 25, which a plain average of 37.5 would miss.
solutions.elegant: There is more of the strong solution, so the answer must exceed the midpoint of 37.5, and only 40 does.

whyOnTest: The plain average is the trap, and noticing which side the answer must fall on eliminates it before any arithmetic.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
